title: Seller Warfare: Tactical Hypotheses & Quick Rebuttals (Sketch)
content:
Context
This is a working sketch for short-form tactical hypotheses that sellers (SEs + AEs) can use during rapid qualification and technical spikes. The idea: 30–90 second hypothesis statements + a 2–3 line diagnostic, then a 15–30s fallback/rebuttal script. Intended for field testing in pilot calls and as seed material for a compact battlecard pack.

Goals
- Speed: get to a clear signal in <90s whether Redwood is a good fit for the integration surface.
- Signal hygiene: separate what matters for cost vs latency vs compliance in one-liners.
- Actionable next steps: each hypothesis includes the next step for SE or engineer to run during a call.

How to use
- Start with the first hypothesis that matches the prospect persona (platform engineer, product lead, security/compliance).
- Deliver the short hypothesis, run the diagnostic, then use the short rebuttal/fallthrough if the answer is not immediately favorable.
- Mark this call with one of three outcome tags: green / amber / red and capture a single anchor metric (e.g., 95th latency target, concurrency need, regulatory boundary).

Hypotheses (canonical format: hypothesis -> quick diagnostic -> if-not-then fallback/rebuttal + next step)

1) Latency-first hypothesis (edge / UX-critical flows)
- Hypothesis: "If you have 95th-percentile latency targets under 300ms for user-facing completions, then we can keep model selection on a low-latency variant + routing to regionally co-located capacity."
- Quick diagnostic: "What's your target for end-to-end completion time in your happy-path UI? Any existing SLOs?"
- If not: "If your target is looser (500–1000ms) we can prioritize cheaper quantized variants and batching; if strict, we can spin a dedicated pool or fractionally reserve capacity for hot routes."
- Next step: capture 95th latency target, estimate per-token budget, log to Jira GTMP-4312 (pilot latency capture).

2) Cost-sensitivity hypothesis (high volume / transactional embedding pipelines)
- Hypothesis: "If you call embeddings at high QPS or batched ingestion, prefix caching + periodic durable embeddings will cut unit cost materially compared to naive calls."
- Quick diagnostic: "Rough monthly document/embedding volume and QPS spikes? Is freshness a hard requirement?"
- If not: "If freshness is flexible we recommend a cached tier + hybrid upsert cadence; if freshness is strict, consider smaller dimensional embeddings or sparser indexing."
- Next step: create a cost-sensitivity sketch (sheet) and schedule 15m with solutions-eng to model cost delta. Link: confluence:INFER-ops-playbook-v2.

3) Compliance/VPC hypothesis (regulated industries)
- Hypothesis: "If your data residency or auditability needs prevent multi-tenant inference, Redwood Private (VPC) or on-prem package is the right fit — with audit trail and KMS integration."
- Quick diagnostic: "Do you need customer-managed KMS, SOC2+ audit bundles, or a completely air-gapped deploy?"
- If not: "If you can accept a dedicated tenancy in our hosted region with strict controls we can keep time-to-value lower; otherwise we'll scope Private in the pilot and set expectations on deployment lead time."
- Next step: open a compliance discovery ticket and request a checklist from security@redwood.

4) Model-fallback resilience hypothesis (reliability at scale)
- Hypothesis: "If you need 99.9% uptime for inference in production, you should plan for multi-variant routing and explicit fallbacks (smaller model family + cached responses) as part of the initial integration."
- Quick diagnostic: "What happens if the model times out or the region is saturated? Any manual fallbacks today?"
- If not: "Recommend a canary and fallback ladder: primary high-quality variant -> secondary smaller variant -> cached last-good -> local heuristic. We can pre-configure this chain in the route policy."
- Next step: draft a route-policy snippet and test with the integration team. Slack: #se-playtesting.

5) Throughput / batchability hypothesis (batch infer + offline)
- Hypothesis: "If your workload is batch-offline or tolerant of 1–2s latencies, batching/compaction + quantized serving can lower compute cost 3–6x with negligible quality loss for many tasks."
- Quick diagnostic: "Is the workload synchronous or can you buffer/async responses? Typical payload sizes?"
- If not: "If strictly synchronous, we prefer continuous batching windows and micro-batching knobs; if async, propose a producer-consumer with caching and dedupe."
- Next step: capture example payload (1–3 sample inputs) and tag for engineering bench test.

Rapid rebuttal snippets (30s ready-to-read)
- "We typically recommend trying a small dedicated pool for the highest-volume route — it removes noisy neighbor risk and gives predictable latency for your top 5% paths."
- "If budget is the blocker, start with a cached prefix tier for the majority of requests and only route the last-mile completions to higher-cost variants."
- "For compliance asks, we can stage a hybrid approach: provision a private control plane while keeping infer compute in our managed region to speed delivery. If they need full air-gap, we'll table that for a scoped Private deployment."

Calibration heuristics for the rep
- Ask for a concrete metric, not vague statements: push for a single SLO (e.g., 95th latency, cost per 1k tokens, or embedding throughput in docs/minute).
- Always convert qualitative objections into a trialable hypothesis + a single next step (e.g., "let's run a 1k request simulator and measure 95th latency").
- Use the fallback ladder language: primary -> cheap-variant -> cached -> heuristic. Keep that ladder front-of-mind.

Conversation traps (things to avoid saying)
- Don't say "any model" or "we have many models" without anchoring on tradeoffs — sellers should tie model family to latency/cost tradeoff quickly.
- Avoid promising exact pricing without a usage sample or pilot; instead commit to a modeled estimate and a follow-up.

Open questions / experiments to run (lab notes)
- Experiment: "90s pilot script" — measure signal captured by SEs in 30 pilot calls (score: binary fit/no-fit + anchor metric). Link results to GTMP-4312.
- Experiment: measure how often fallback ladder triggers in 5 customer pilots when we enable the ladder vs when we don't.
- Engage with product-hosted-api on two quick defaults for route-policy templates for SEs to deploy during pilots. (Ping: Renee).

Appendix: short templates sellers can paste on calls
- Quick starter: "We typically benchmark by asking for one anchor metric — what's your acceptable 95th latency? If <300ms, we'll lean on low-latency variants and co-located pools; if >500ms we can optimize for cost. Can you share a target?"
- Quick follow: "If budget is the constraint, we can set up a cached-tier test that routes X% of requests to a cached response to validate quality drop before we scale."

Notes to self
- This is intentionally terse; we should convert high-signal snippets into 6x micro-cards (30s each) for the seller pocket deck.
- Next: pair with SEs Diego and Owen to run 10 live calls and collect real transcripts (anonymized) by 2025-01-31.
